To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

RV nucleotide substitutions are more rapid than previously reported and that the differences in substitution rates between regions of the genome are largely explained by temporal biases in the sampling of sequences.
the substitution rates of rubella virus are high, but that temporal sampling biases and selection acting on RNA structure have important effects on substitution rate estimates.

RV nucleotide sites with biologically functional secondary structure have lower substitution rates, RV nucleotide substitution rate is higher at the 3′ end than at the 5′ end of the genome, and RV nucleotide substitution is faster in the E1 gene than in the P150 gene.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of analytical tools for the study of RV evolution and epidemiology.
the impact of secondary structure on the estimation of nucleotide substitution rates and the use of such rates to date RV sequences.

the impact of temporal sampling biases, recombination and selection on nucleotide substitution rate estimation in rubella virus and the implications of these findings for future attempts to eradicate RV.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the RV substitution rate is high but variable and that the substitution rate of the RV genome is likely to be underestimated by the current estimates.
the nucleotide substitution rate of rubella virus is 1.19-7.52 ×10-3 substitutions per site per year, with a mean value of 3.5 ×10-3.
RV is a very rapidly evolving RNA virus with high substitution rates across its genome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed an analytical approach that can be used to estimate nucleotide substitution rate in viruses with high recombination rates and/or with a high proportion of secondary structure in their genomes.
we provide a detailed analysis of RV nucleotide substitution rate estimation and we provide a framework for future analyses that will allow us to monitor the global spread and decline of RV.
the nucleotide substitution rates of RV are higher than previously thought and that the secondary structure is a key element in the evolution of RV.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the RV nucleotide substitution rate is not uniform across the entire RV genome, and the rate of nucleotide substitution in the RV genome is influenced by both temporal sampling biases and natural selection favour

the use of RV nucleotide substitution rate data to monitor the global RV decline will require a careful assessment of temporal sampling biases and the possible influence of purifying selection on RV nucleotide substitution estimates.
the use of RV genomic sequence data for the estimation of nucleotide substitution rates should be undertaken with caution, particularly when the dataset is temporally biased.
